parole.significato: A Ukrainian grandmother.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian бабу́ся (babúsja).

parole.significato: A member of, or one who subscribes to the ideas of, the political movement of Stepan Bandera.
parole.testo: First attested in 1951. Borrowed from Ukrainian банде́рівець (bandérivecʹ) + -ite, from the surname of Stepan Bandera, a Ukrainian nationalist leader. Compare Russian банде́ровец (bandɛ́rovec).

parole.significato: A Ukrainian plucked stringed instrument with a tear-shaped body, like an asymmetrical lute or a vertical zither, which…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian банду́ра (bandúra), possibly through Italian pandura and Polish bandura, from Late Latin pandura (“musical instrument with three strings”), from Ancient Greek πανδοῦρα (pandoûra, “three-stringed lute; zither”), perhaps from Lydian.

parole.significato: A fool.
parole.testo: From Ukrainian баня́к (banják, “cooking pot”).

parole.significato: Any member of an ethnolinguistic group native to the Carpathians’ Eastern Beskyds who speak a dialect of Rusyn and are…
parole.testo: From Ukrainian бо́йко (bójko).

parole.significato: Any of several species of large bee in the genus Bombus.
parole.testo: 1520s from bumble + bee, replacing Middle English humbul-be. Merged with Middle English bombeln (“to boom, buzz”), in the late 14th century. The name of the drink is a semantic loan from Ukrainian джміль (džmilʹ).

parole.significato: The controversial practice of forced conscription of draft-age men in public in Ukraine during the Russo-Ukraine war.
parole.testo: Calque of Ukrainian бусифіка́ція (busyfikácija). Can be analysed as bus + -ification, referring to the use of buses to force draft-age men in Ukraine to fight against the Russian invasion.

parole.significato: A Ukrainian decoration made from sheaves of wheat tied up with colorful ribbons, which is used in rituals around Christ…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian діду́х (didúx), from дід (did, “grandfather”) + -ух (-ux, augmentative suffix).

parole.significato: Of or associated with Dnipro (a city in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, Ukraine).
parole.testo: From Dnipr + -ian via Ukrainian Дніпро́ (Dnipró, “Dnipro city”).

parole.significato: native female resident of Dnipro
parole.testo: Calque of Ukrainian дніпря́нка (dniprjánka)

parole.significato: native male resident of Dnipro
parole.testo: Calque of Ukrainian дніпря́нин (dniprjányn)

parole.significato: In Ukrainian folklore, a spirit of a house who protects the inhabitants.
parole.testo: From Ukrainian домови́к (domovýk).

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to the city of Drohobych in Ukraine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian Дрого́бич (Drohóbyč).

parole.significato: A genre of instrumental folk music from Ukraine.
parole.testo: From Ukrainian ду́мка (dúmka), diminutive of ду́ма (dúma, “sung epic poem”).

parole.significato: Underwear, especially men's briefs.
parole.testo: Variation of gotch, from Ukrainian га́чі (háči), ґа́чі (gáči).

parole.significato: A type of hydric soil, sticky, greenish-blue-grey in colour and low in oxygen.
parole.testo: 1920s, from Ukrainian ґлей (glej, “clayey soil”), from Proto-Slavic *glьjь, from Proto-Indo-European *gl̥h₁y-ó-s, from Proto-Indo-European *gleh₁y-. Cognate of clay.

parole.significato: Men's brief-style underwear.
parole.testo: From gitch, a variation of gotch, from Ukrainian га́чі (háči), ґа́чі pl (gáči).

parole.significato: Men's underwear.
parole.testo: From Ukrainian га́чі (háči), ґа́чі pl (gáči, “underwear”). Possibly back-formed from diminutive gotchies.

parole.significato: a Ukrainian (often Cossack) insurgent against Poland-Lithuania in the 18th century.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian гайдамака (hajdamaka), ultimately from Ottoman Turkish هايدامق (haydamak), probably from the Ottoman Turkish هایده (hayde), combined with the Ottoman Turkish ـمق (-mak), possibly under influence of Ukrainian -ак (-ak), related to haydamak.

parole.significato: cabbage rolls.
parole.testo: From Ukrainian го́лубці (hólubci), singular голубе́ць (holubécʹ). Doublet of golubtsy.

parole.significato: A Ukrainian national dance in 2/4 time.
parole.testo: 1925–30, from Ukrainian гопа́к (hopák), from the interjection гоп (hop). Compare Ukrainian го́пати (hópaty), го́пкати (hópkaty), гопцюва́ти (hopcjuváty), го́пки (hópky), and dated Ukrainian го́пи (hópy, “dance steps”), го́пка (hópka, “child (jocular)”).

parole.significato: Ukrainian distilled spirit, sometimes flavoured with hot peppers.
parole.testo: From Ukrainian горі́лка (horílka, “vodka”). Compare Belarusian гарэ́лка (harélka), South Russian горе́лка (gorélka).

parole.significato: A basic unit of administrative division in Ukraine, similar to a municipality.
parole.testo: From Ukrainian грома́да (hromáda, “community”).

parole.significato: The currency of Ukraine, symbol ₴, divided into 100 kopiykas.
parole.testo: From Ukrainian гри́вня (hrývnja). Doublet of grivna and grzywna.

parole.significato: The monetary unit of Ukraine from 1917 to 1920, 1942 to 1945, and 1991 to 1996.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian карбованець (karbovanecʹ).

parole.significato: A Russian, especially from a Ukrainian perspective.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Ukrainian каца́п (kacáp) (see it for more).

parole.significato: A lute-like stringed instrument traditionally made from a single block of wood, with a medium-length neck, originating…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian ко́бза (kóbza), itself from Proto-Turkic *kopuŕ. Doublet of komuz and cobza.

parole.significato: An itinerant Ukrainian bard, often blind, who played the kobza
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian кобзар (kobzar).

parole.significato: A collective farm in the former Soviet Union; a kolkhoz.
parole.testo: From Ukrainian колго́сп m (kolhósp), plural колго́спи pl (kolhóspy), contraction of Ukrainian колекти́вне господа́рство n (kolektývne hospodárstvo, “collective farm”).

parole.significato: A Ukrainian and Russian couple-dance with constantly increasing tempo.
parole.testo: From Ukrainian or Russian козачо́к (kozačók), diminutive of коза́к (kozák, “Cossack”), because the dance originated among Cossacks.

parole.significato: A smoked pork sausage with garlic, originating in Eastern Europe.
parole.testo: From Ukrainian ковбаса́ (kovbasá /⁠kowbasˈa⁠/, “sausage”, see there for more), a very early Slavic borrowing with no clear antecedent. The Slavic variants (including Polish kiełbasa, whence kielbasa) point to several reconstructed forms from Proto-Slavic *kъlbasa, *klobasa, *kobasa. It is considered

parole.significato: A rich or supposedly rich peasant, targeted during Soviet collectivization, especially in the context of Ukraine or Ukr…
parole.testo: From Ukrainian куркуль (kurkulʹ, “frightening and dangerous one”), куркулі pl (kurkuli).

parole.significato: Of or associated with the city of Kyiv (the capital city of Ukraine).
parole.testo: From Kyiv + -an, from Ukrainian Ки́їв (Kýjiv).

parole.significato: Of, from or pertaining to Kyiv.
parole.testo: From Kyiv + -ite, from Ukrainian Ки́їв (Kýjiv).

parole.significato: A Ukrainian flat-woven rug or tapestry; kilim.
parole.testo: Borrowing of Ukrainian килим (kylym), influenced by English kilim.

parole.significato: A Ukrainian folk musical instrument similar to the hurdy-gurdy.
parole.testo: From Ukrainian ліра (lira), ultimately related to the Byzantine lyra (Ancient Greek λύρα (lúra)). Doublet of Lyra, lyra, and lyre.

parole.significato: An itinerant Ukrainian musician who performed religious, historical and epic songs to the accompaniment of a lira, the…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian лірник (lirnyk).

parole.significato: Independence Square, the main city square in Kyiv, Ukraine.
parole.testo: From Майда́н Незале́жності (Majdán Nezaléžnosti, “Independence Square”) in Kiev, from Ukrainian майда́н (majdán, “square”), from Ottoman Turkish میدان (meydan), from the same Persian source as above.

parole.significato: A Ukrainian clay mixing bowl used to grind various soft products.
parole.testo: From Ukrainian макі́тра (makítra).

parole.significato: In Ukrainian folklore, a forest spirit who lures men to their deaths.
parole.testo: From Ukrainian ма́вка (mávka).

parole.significato: a Russian; a Russki
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian моска́ль (moskálʹ).

parole.significato: Synonym of nalesnik in Ukrainian cuisine.
parole.testo: From Ukrainian нали́сник (nalýsnyk). Doublet of nalesnik and nalistnik.

parole.significato: Of, from, or relating to Odesa (a city in Ukraine).
parole.testo: From Odesa + -ite, from Ukrainian одесит (odesyt). Compare Ukrainian Одеса (Odesa).

parole.significato: A small savory or sweet yeast-raised bun or doughnut typical for Ukrainian cuisine.
parole.testo: From Ukrainian пампу́шка (pampúška).

parole.significato: A type of Ukrainian dumpling, similar to Polish pierogi. Traditionally called pyrohy or varenyky.
parole.testo: A mondegreen of Ukrainian пироги (pyrohy). The “d” in spelling is probably due to intervocalic flapping.

parole.significato: A type of flanged mace from medieval Kievan Rus'.
parole.testo: Ukrainian перна́ч (pernáč), пірна́ч (pirnáč).

parole.significato: Synonym of pierogi in Ukrainian cuisine.
parole.testo: From Ukrainian пироги́ (pyrohý), plural of пирі́г (pyríh). Doublet of pierogi (from Polish), pirogi (from Russian), and pirohy (from Czech and Slovak).

parole.significato: A hand-decorated Ukrainian Easter egg with intricate designs.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian пи́санка (pýsanka), from писа́ти (pysáty, “to write”), referring to writing on an egg with a stylus in a wax-resist dyeing process, from Proto-Slavic *pьsati, related to *pьstrъ (“feathered”), + feminine ending -ка (-ka).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Ruscism (“Russian fascism”).
parole.testo: From Ukrainian раши́ст (rašýst), itself a blend of Ра́ша (Ráša, “Russia”) (derogatory) + фаши́ст (fašýst, “fascist”).

parole.significato: A type of East Slavic yogurt-like beverage made from baked milk.
parole.testo: From Ukrainian ря́жанка (rjážanka).

parole.significato: Samizdat.
parole.testo: 1971, from Ukrainian самви́дав (samvýdav, “samizdat”) < сам (sam, “self”) + ви́дання (výdannja, “publication”). Compare samizdat < Russian самизда́т (samizdát).

parole.significato: a Cossack soldier who serves as a mercenary for the hetman under the Zaporizhian Army.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian сердю́к (serdjúk), in turn originated from Ottoman Turkish سورتوك (“streetwalker, dirty vagrant”). Compare Turkish sürtük.

parole.significato: A Ukrainian monetary unit.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian шаг (šah).

parole.significato: Stereotypical depictions of Ukrainian culture and people.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian шарова́рщина (šarovárščyna).

parole.significato: An administrative and military centre for the Zaporozhian and Danube Cossacks.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian Січ (Sič), from Ukrainian сікти (sikty, “to chop”), alluding to the clearing of a forest for an encampment, or the building of a fort with trees that have been cut down.

parole.significato: A місце́ва ра́да (mistseva rada) centred in a village (село́) or, historically, a rural-type settlement (се́лище [сільс…
parole.testo: From Ukrainian сільра́да (silʹráda), a clipped compound of сільська́ ра́да (silʹsʹká ráda), itself also borrowed into English as silska rada.

parole.significato: Synonym of silrada
parole.testo: From Ukrainian сільська́ ра́да (silʹsʹká ráda). Doublet of silrada.

parole.significato: Synonym of syrnik in Ukrainian cuisine.
parole.testo: From Ukrainian си́рник (sýrnyk). Doublet of syrnik.

parole.significato: A Ukrainian limited liability company.
parole.testo: From Ukrainian ТОВ (TOV), initialism of товари́ство з обмéженою відповідáльністю (tovarýstvo z obméženoju vidpovidálʹnistju)

parole.significato: A trident emblem representing Ukraine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian тризу́б (tryzúb, “trident”), from три (try, “three”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes (“three”)) + зуб (zub, “tooth”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵómbʰos (“tooth; row of teeth; peg”)). See three, comb.

parole.significato: The Ukrainian version of the hammered dulcimer.
parole.testo: Ukrainian цимбали (cymbaly)

parole.significato: Literature on the subject of Ukraine or Ukrainian people, especially regarding Ukrainian culture, language, or literatu…
parole.testo: First appears c. 1944, from Ukrainian украї́ніка (ukrajínika), influenced by Latin ukrainica.

parole.significato: A cold Ukrainian beverage made from boiled fruits (typically fresh or dried).
parole.testo: From Ukrainian узвар (uzvar). Doublet of vzvar.

parole.significato: Boiled dumplings stuffed with potato, cheese, or other filling; a serving of these; plural of varenyk.
parole.testo: From Ukrainian варе́ники pl (varényky), singular варе́ник (varényk), and related terms in other languages, e.g. Russian варе́ники (varéniki) and (particularly in Mennonite communities) Plautdietsch Wareniki. The Ukrainian term comes from ва́рений (várenyj, “boiled”), from вари́ти (varýty, “to boil,

parole.significato: A traditional Ukrainian wreath chiefly decorated with flowers and other plant parts, which is worn by women and girls a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian віно́к (vinók), from Old East Slavic вѣнъкъ (věnŭkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *věnъkъ, from *věnъ (“wreath”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weh₁y- (“to plait, twist, weave, wind”)) + *-ъkъ (diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: Small dumplings from Ukrainian cuisine, typically filled with mushrooms and served in borshch at Christmas Eve dinner.
parole.testo: From Ukrainian ву́шка (vúška), plural of ву́шко (vúško, “little ear”), diminutive of ву́хо (vúxo, “ear”).

parole.significato: Traditional Ukrainian and Belarusian clothing, featuring elements of Ukrainian and Belarusian ethnic embroidery.
parole.testo: From Ukrainian вишива́нка (vyšyvánka). Compare Belarusian вышыва́нка (vyšyvánka).
